client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. I can't seem to focus on any of my university work — I'll sit down to read or write something and my mind just goes blank, or I end up thinking about her instead. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, honestly, because nothing is going to bring her back.
therapist: What you're carrying right now is so heavy, and I can hear in the quietness of your voice just how exhausted and hollowed out this grief has left you. You're absolutely right that nothing will bring her back, and I don't want to pretend otherwise — but what we can work on together is helping you find a way to hold this loss without it completely shutting you out of your own life. The fact that your mind keeps drifting to her isn't a failure of focus; it's a sign of how much she meant to you, and that's actually a meaningful place for us to start.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess that's a slightly different way to look at it — I've mostly just been beating myself up for being so distracted and falling behind on my coursework. But I'm still not sure how talking about her is going to make it any easier to actually sit down and get through a reading or write an essay. It just feels like two completely separate things.
therapist: The way you're speaking — quickly, with a kind of tension in your voice — tells me there's a real urgency here, like part of you is trying to hold everything together while also feeling quite lost. That self-criticism you mentioned, beating yourself up for being distracted, is actually a really important connection to your coursework struggles — because when our mind is consumed by grief *and* by harsh self-judgment, there's very little mental space left for reading or writing. So in a way, these two things aren't as separate as they feel; understanding what's happening emotionally can actually start to loosen that mental block.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Okay, I can see the logic in what you're saying, and maybe you're right that they're connected somehow. But even if I understand that emotionally, I don't really know how that translates into actually being able to concentrate when I have a deadline staring me down. It feels like knowing the reason for something doesn't automatically fix it.
therapist: You're making a really valid point, and I notice there's still a kind of urgency in your voice even as you're trying to reason this through — which makes sense, because understanding something intellectually and actually *feeling* relief are two very different things. You're right that insight alone doesn't fix concentration, so in CBT we'd also work on very concrete, practical strategies — like breaking tasks into smaller steps and gently redirecting that self-critical voice when it shows up at your desk. It's not about waiting until the grief feels resolved before you can function; it's about building small moments of capacity alongside the grief, rather than fighting it.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: The idea of breaking tasks into smaller steps sounds reasonable on paper, but I've tried that kind of thing before and when I'm actually sitting there, even the smallest step feels overwhelming because my mind just fills up with thoughts of her. And then I feel guilty for even trying to do coursework, like I'm somehow moving on or forgetting her by attempting to be productive. I don't know how you're supposed to "gently redirect" that when the guilt is so loud.
therapist: The way you're speaking — very quietly, with a kind of fragility in your voice — tells me this guilt is something you're carrying very tenderly, almost like you're afraid to disturb it. That belief that being productive means forgetting her is such a painful and understandable thought, but it's also worth gently questioning — because your grandmother being important to you isn't stored in your inability to work; it lives in you regardless of whether you're reading an essay or grieving. Doing your coursework isn't a betrayal of her; it might even be something she would have wanted for you.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client: That last part actually hit me a bit harder than I expected, because she did always push me to do well in my studies — she was really proud of me for getting into university. But it also feels almost too convenient, like I'm just telling myself a comforting story to make the guilt go away rather than actually dealing with it. I'm not sure if that's the same thing as genuinely believing it.
therapist: The softness in your voice right now, sitting alongside that very thoughtful, almost cautious way you're working through this, tells me you're genuinely wrestling with something important rather than just looking for an easy out — and that instinct to question whether something is "too convenient" is actually a sign of real intellectual honesty, not resistance. But there's a difference between a comforting *distortion* and a comforting *truth* — and in CBT, we'd ask: what's the actual evidence that your grandmother was proud of you and wanted you to succeed? If that evidence is real, then believing it isn't a trick you're playing on yourself; it's simply allowing yourself to hold something true. The goal isn't to make the guilt disappear, but to slowly loosen its grip by testing whether it's actually telling you something accurate.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: The evidence is real — she came to my enrollment day, she kept a photo of my university acceptance letter on her fridge, she used to tell her friends about me studying there. I can't really argue with any of that. But sitting here acknowledging it just makes me miss her more acutely, and I'm not sure I'm ready to use those memories as a kind of tool to push through my coursework — it feels like it might cheapen them somehow.
therapist: The softness and quiet in your voice right now feels very tender, like you're holding something precious and fragile — and I want to honour that, because what you just shared about her isn't a tool or a technique; it's love, and it makes complete sense that accessing it brings both comfort and pain at the same time. You don't have to use those memories *instrumentally* to get through a deadline — but perhaps they don't need to be kept separate from your studies either; she can simply be *with* you as you work, the way she always was when she was proud of you. That's not cheapening the memories — that's carrying her forward.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: "Carrying her forward" — I don't know why that phrase is getting to me, but it is. I think part of me has been treating grief like I have to stay still inside it to prove I loved her, and maybe that's been making everything harder. I'm still not sure how this is going to look in practice when I'm staring at a blank page at midnight with a deadline the next day, but I think I understand something slightly differently now than I did when I walked in here.
therapist: The softness and quiet in your voice right now feels like something has genuinely shifted — not dramatically, but in that deep, still way that real insight sometimes arrives. What you just named — that staying frozen in grief felt like proof of love — is such an important recognition, and it took real courage to get there today. And for those midnight moments with the blank page, we can work on that together practically, but you've already given yourself something more important to hold onto than a technique.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I appreciate you saying that, and I do feel like something is slightly different, though I'm also a little wary of leaving here feeling okay and then falling apart again the moment I'm back in my flat alone with my books. I think the loneliness of it is a big part of what makes those late-night moments so hard — there's no one there to remind me of any of this, and it's easy to forget what felt true in a room like this. I'm not sure how to hold onto something that feels this fragile when I'm on my own.
therapist: There's something in your voice right now — a kind of breathless vulnerability, like you're already anticipating that loneliness before you've even left — and I want you to know that fear is completely understandable, but it's also worth noticing that *you* were the one who found that insight today, not me. One practical thing we can do is help you create a small anchor for those late-night moments — something as simple as a few words you write down before you leave here today, in your own handwriting, that can speak back to you when the room feels empty and the grief feels loud. What felt true here didn't come from this room; it came from you, and that means you can take it with you.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Writing something down feels almost too simple for how complicated this all feels, and part of me worries I'll just look at the words and they'll seem hollow when I'm actually in that dark place. But I think I want to try it anyway, even if I'm skeptical — maybe something like "she wanted this for you" or "carrying her forward," because those are the things that actually landed today. I just hope that when I'm alone and it's late and I'm exhausted, some version of me will actually remember to look at it instead of just spiraling.
therapist: The way you're speaking — softly but quickly, like you're trying to get this out before the doubt catches up with you — tells me that the part of you that wants to try is real, even if the skeptical part is loud right now. Those words you chose — *her* words, really, reflected back through you — aren't arbitrary; they landed because they're true, and there may be a version of you at midnight who needs exactly that simplicity rather than something more complicated. And the fact that you're already thinking about how to take care of that future, exhausted version of yourself — that's not a small thing; that's you beginning to carry yourself forward too.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That phrase "carrying yourself forward too" is doing something unexpected to me, because I think I've been so focused on not abandoning her that I hadn't really considered that I might also be abandoning myself in the process. I'm not sure I fully know what it looks like to take care of myself right now, especially when it still feels a bit selfish to even think that way. But I think that might be something worth sitting with, even if it makes me uncomfortable.
therapist: The speed and pitch in your voice right now tells me this realisation arrived with a kind of urgency, like something cracking open that's been held tightly shut for a long time — and I want to gently stay with you in that, because what you just named is profound. The idea that self-care is selfish is one of grief's cruellest tricks, but your grandmother wasn't proud of a version of you that was disappearing; she was proud of *you*, which means taking care of yourself is part of honouring her, not betraying her. That discomfort you're willing to sit with — that's not a problem to solve today; that might be the most important thing you take home with you.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech
